summary_plain: The SAFFIRE-I investigation burned large fabric samples inside an uncrewed cargo vehicle after it departed from the International Space Station to study how fires grow in microgravity. Researchers used a composite material made of cotton and fiberglass to simulate clothing and other cabin materials. Understanding how flames spread and how materials burn in space helps engineers design safer spacecraft and protect astronauts on future exploration missions.
summary_expert: The SAFFIRE-I experiment was conducted on an Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after deberthing from the ISS to investigate large-scale fire growth and low-gravity flammability limits. The test burned a composite fabric sample called Sibal, consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by weight, measuring approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide. The experiment module featured a flow duct where air was drawn at a velocity of 20 cm/s by top-mounted fans. Instrumentation captured flame images, temperatures, radiation, pressure, gas mole fractions, and flow velocities, providing large-scale microgravity combustion data to anchor ground-based models and validate material selection criteria.

key_findings.text: The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by weight.
The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric.
Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.
